name: Ancient Greece
capital: No single capital (Athens, Sparta, Corinth, Thebes…)
summary: A world of rival city-states that pioneered democracy (Athens), philosophy, theatre and science, and spread Greek culture across the Mediterranean.

knownFor.label: Hoplite phalanx
knownFor.note: Citizen soldiers with large round shields fighting in close ranks.

knownFor.label: Parthenon
knownFor.note: Temple to Athena on the Acropolis.

knownFor.label: Olympic Games
knownFor.note: Athletic festival held at Olympia every four years.

location.value: Centred on the northeastern Mediterranean (Greece, the Aegean islands, western Anatolia), with colonies from the Black Sea to Spain.

terrain.value: Mountainous terrain split the land into many small regions and valleys, each with its own dialect and identity, which encouraged independent city-states. The sea connected them.

climate.value: Mediterranean: dry summers and wet winters, suited to olives, vines and grain.
climate.source: Ober, The Rise and Fall of Classical Greece (2015)

resources.value: Olive oil, wine, silver (Athens’ Laurion mines, worked by slaves), marble and timber. Grain often had to be imported.

disasters.value: The plague of Athens (430–426 BCE), which killed Pericles. Earthquakes, such as the one that struck Sparta around 464 BCE.

population.value: Rose about tenfold between 800 and 400 BCE, from roughly 800,000 to 7.5–10 million (one estimate).

urbanisation.value: Hundreds of poleis (city-states). Athens was the largest classical city. Later, Hellenistic cities like Alexandria became huge.

disease.value: The plague of Athens during the Peloponnesian War (from 430 BCE) killed perhaps a quarter of the city.

migration.value: Colonisation (c. 750–500 BCE) founded cities such as Syracuse, Naples, Marseille and Byzantium (Istanbul).

economicBase.value: Farming (olives, vines, grain), crafts, silver mining and sea trade. Living standards in classical Athens were high for the ancient world.

tradeRoutes.value: Mediterranean and Black Sea trade linking city-states and colonies. Grain imports from the Black Sea and Egypt.

wealth.value: Urban wages in 5th–4th century Athens were high (7–12 kg of wheat a day for unskilled workers), suggesting strong economic growth.
wealth.source: Wikipedia: Ancient Greece (checked 5 Nov 2026); Ober, The Rise and Fall of Classical Greece (2015)

moneyAndTax.value: Coinage was adopted in the Archaic period (silver Athenian “owls”). Athens taxed its empire’s allies (Delian League tribute) and wealthy citizens (liturgies).

inequality.value: Free citizens, resident foreigners (metics), and large numbers of slaves. Between 40% and 80% of classical Athens’ population may have been enslaved, depending on the estimate.

governmentType.value: Hundreds of independent city-states with varied systems: democracy (Athens), mixed oligarchy with two kings (Sparta), tyrannies and monarchies. Unified only once, 338–323 BCE, under Macedon.

keyRulers.value: Solon (reforms, 594 BCE). Cleisthenes (democracy, c. 508 BCE). Pericles (Athens’ golden age, d. 429 BCE). Philip II of Macedon. Alexander the Great (336–323 BCE).

succession.value: Varied by city: elected and lot-chosen officials in Athens, hereditary dual kingship in Sparta, dynasties in Macedon and the Hellenistic kingdoms.

institutions.value: Athenian democracy (the assembly, the council, courts with citizen juries) was the world’s first democracy, open only to adult male citizens. Draco’s law code (621 BCE). The Olympic Games.

stability.value: Frequent wars between cities, civil strife (stasis) and short-lived regimes such as the Thirty Tyrants in Athens (404–403 BCE).

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry between rich and poor and between democratic and oligarchic factions, especially during the Peloponnesian War.

armyAndTech.value: Heavy infantry citizen-soldiers (hoplites) in phalanxes, and trireme warships (Athens had over 200). Macedon added the long-spear phalanx and cavalry.

majorWars.value: The Greco-Persian Wars (Marathon 490, Salamis 480, Plataea 479 BCE). The Peloponnesian War (431–404 BCE) between Athens and Sparta. Philip II’s victory at Chaeronea (338 BCE). Alexander’s conquests (334–323 BCE).

territoryChange.value: Greek culture spread across the Mediterranean by colonisation, then across the Middle East to India with Alexander. Absorbed by Rome (Corinth destroyed 146 BCE, Ptolemaic Egypt annexed 30 BCE).

alliancesRivals.value: The Delian League (led by Athens) against the Peloponnesian League (led by Sparta). Persia as common enemy and later paymaster. Macedon and then Rome.

inventions.value: The Greek alphabet (adapted from Phoenician), theatre, geometry and scientific astronomy (Aristarchus’ Sun-centred model, Eratosthenes measuring the Earth), and Hellenistic engineering.

scienceEducation.value: Philosophy (Socrates, Plato’s Academy, Aristotle’s Lyceum), medicine (Hippocrates), history (Herodotus, Thucydides). Schooling was mostly private, for boys from age seven.

openness.value: Borrowed from Egypt and the Near East (the alphabet, mathematics, art styles) and spread its own culture widely through colonies and conquest.

religion.value: Polytheistic, with the Twelve Olympian gods, animal sacrifice, oracles (Delphi) and festivals.

languageWriting.value: Ancient Greek in several dialects, written in the Greek alphabet. Homer’s epics were first passed down orally.

artsArchitecture.value: The Parthenon (447–432 BCE), classical sculpture, tragedy and comedy (Sophocles, Aristophanes), lyric poetry, and Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey.

socialStructure.value: Citizens (male), women (excluded from politics), metics, and slaves. Sparta relied on an enslaved population, the helots, who were freed in Messenia in 370/369 BCE.

sharedIdentity.value: Despite political division, Greeks (Hellenes) shared a language, religion, the Olympic Games and the idea of being distinct from “barbarians”.

neighbours.value: Persia, Phoenicians and Carthage, Egypt, Thracians, Scythians, Etruscans and Rome.

ideasReligions.value: Often called the “cradle of Western civilisation”. Its philosophy, science, art and political ideas shaped Rome, Byzantium, the Islamic world and Europe.

colonisation.value: As colonisers, Greeks founded independent colonies around the Mediterranean and Black Sea (c. 750–500 BCE). Later Greece was itself conquered by Macedon and Rome.

riseSignals.value: After the Dark Ages (c. 1100–750 BCE), city-states formed in the 8th century BCE. Population grew, colonies spread, trade revived, and the alphabet was adopted.

peakPeriod.value: The Classical period (c. 500–323 BCE), especially the Golden Age of Athens in the mid-5th century BCE.

declineSignals.value: The ruinous Peloponnesian War, constant inter-city wars, and the rise of Macedon.

outcome.value: Conquest and transformation. Macedon dominated from 338 BCE, Rome conquered Greece (146 BCE) and the last Hellenistic kingdom (30 BCE). Greek culture lived on in Rome and the Byzantine Empire.

sources.value: Greek historians (Herodotus, Thucydides, Xenophon), inscriptions, archaeology and literature. Most sources are Athenian, so Athens is best documented. Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026. See also Ober (2015).

overallCertainty.value: Good for major events. Period boundaries vary by source (e.g. the Dark Ages c. 1100–750 BCE; the Hellenistic end in 31 or 30 BCE). Population and slavery shares are estimates.
